exercises.label: Exercise 7.B1 — Medium: A looser temperature cap may not help
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The relaxed-cap answer defines K0, follows the synchronous pruning rule to remove62 in the first round and60 in the second, and explains why60 initially survived. It verifies at least one surviving action for every remaining state and the fixed point K3=K2, establishing maximal continued feasibility rather than just a safe subset. The unchanged interlock and the practical difference between delaying failure and sustaining operation are explicit.
exercises.replacement_html:
1. Start with all states satisfying the relaxed cap. The candidate set is $K_0=\{52,54,56,58,60,62\}$ degrees. A pruning round keeps a state only if an available action has a successor in the current candidate set. At $62$, cooling is forbidden by the unchanged interlock and running gives $64$, outside $K_0$. Thus the first round removes $62$ and gives $K_1=\{52,54,56,58,60\}$.

2. Propagate the loss of continuation backward. State $60$ survived the first round because running to $62$ was still in $K_0$. But now its only available successor, $62$, is outside $K_1$. The second round removes $60$, leaving $K_2=\{52,54,56,58\}$.

3. Verify the fixed point state by state. Running sends $52$ to $54$ and $54$ to $56$. At $56$, running reaches $58$ and cooling reaches $52$. At $58$, cooling reaches $54$. Each surviving state therefore has at least one successor in $K_2$, so $K_3=K_2$. Following these choices gives an indefinitely safe continuation, and the removed states have none. Hence the viability kernel is exactly $\{52,54,56,58\}$, unchanged from the original cap.

The relaxed instantaneous limit allows a doomed trajectory one more step, but it supplies no sustainable action at high temperatures. Changing the cooling interlock or capacity would change the transition model; raising the temperature cap alone does not solve that controllability obstruction.

exercises.label: Exercise 7.B2 — Hard: Recompute the penalty after changing the horizon preference
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The current answer derives the penalty threshold correctly but asserts that the alternative cooling detour at56 is worse without comparing its discounted rewards, and compresses the threshold fraction rearrangement. Add the actual same-state three-step route comparison, safe Bellman values, complete unsafe return, inequality algebra and equality/24 checks so the optimal-action conclusion follows step by step.
exercises.replacement_html:
Determine the best safe continuation before choosing a penalty. At $58$ degrees, staying viable requires cooling to $54$ with reward $0$. At $54$, running reaches $56$ with reward $3$. At $56$, both running to $58$ and cooling to $52$ are viable, so this last choice needs a reward comparison.

Starting at $56$, the running route $56\to58\to54\to56$ has rewards $(3,0,3)$. The cooling route $56\to52\to54\to56$ has rewards $(0,3,3)$. Both return to the same state after three steps. If $V_{56}$ denotes the best safe return from that state afterward, their values are

$$\begin{aligned} R_{56}&=3+\gamma\,0+\gamma^2\,3+\gamma^3V_{56},\\ C_{56}&=0+\gamma\,3+\gamma^2\,3+\gamma^3V_{56},\\ R_{56}-C_{56}&=3(1-\gamma)=3(0.2)=0.6\gt0. \end{aligned}$$

Thus running is the best safe choice at $56$. The best safe cycle from $58$ is consequently $58\to54\to56\to58$, with rewards $(0,3,3)$.

Sum the continuing safe cycle at the new discount. Write its return from $58$ as $V_s$. Returning to $58$ after three steps adds the same future value with weight $\gamma^3$:

$$\begin{aligned} V_s&=0+0.8(3)+0.8^2(3)+0.8^3V_s\\ &=2.4+1.92+0.512V_s,\\ (1-0.512)V_s&=4.32,\\ V_s&=\frac{4.32}{0.488}=\frac{4320}{488}=\frac{540}{61}\approx8.852459. \end{aligned}$$

Include the full unsafe route and the timing of its penalty. Running at $58$ earns $25$ immediately and reaches $60$. Cooling is unavailable at $60$, so running one step later earns $3$ and incurs the one-time failure penalty $p$. There is zero return after failure. Hence

$$U_p=25+0.8(3-p)=27.4-0.8p.$$

For every optimal action at $58$ to be safe, the unsafe action must be strictly worse, rather than merely tied. Solve $U_p\lt V_s$:

$$\begin{aligned} 27.4-0.8p&\lt\frac{540}{61}\\ 0.8p&\gt27.4-\frac{540}{61}\\ p&\gt\frac{137/5-540/61}{4/5} =\frac{5657/305}{4/5} =\frac{5657}{244}\approx23.184426. \end{aligned}$$

The division preserves the direction because $0.8\gt0$. At penalties above this threshold, the safe Bellman values are $V_{58}=540/61$, $V_{56}=3+0.8V_{58}=615/61$, $V_{54}=3+0.8V_{56}=675/61$, and $V_{52}=3+0.8V_{54}=723/61$. At $56$, cooling gives $0.8V_{52}$, which is $0.6$ less than running; at $52$ or $54$, cooling immediately fails with reward $-p\lt0$, whereas running has a positive value. At $58$, the displayed strict inequality makes cooling preferable to its complete unsafe continuation. Thus these comparisons check all competing actions, rather than assuming that a later unsafe departure or a cooling detour creates a better policy.

Evaluate the requested penalty and the boundary case. At $p=24$, $U_p=27.4-0.8(24)=27.4-19.2=8.2$, below $540/61\approx8.852459$. Cooling is the unique maximizing action at $58$ in this model. At the exact threshold $p=5657/244$, $U_p=V_s$: immediate unsafe running and cooling with the best continuation both maximize return. Therefore the claim that every optimal action is safe fails at equality.

The threshold concerns this exact discounted finite-state reward model. The smaller discount gives the delayed failure penalty less weight, so it needs a larger numerical penalty than at $\gamma=0.9$. Directly forbidding transitions out of the viability kernel is a different safety mechanism; a guessed penalty does not replace the comparison above.

exercises.label: Exercise 7.P1 — Easy: Safe now, but doomed next
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The correct verbal classification can be made more traceable at this first easy exercise by showing the initial nonfailure set, its one-round pruning and fixed point, then testing both actions at A against the resulting kernel and the two-step failure of go.
exercises.replacement_html:
Start from states that have not already failed. The failure set is $\{F\}$, so the initial candidate safe set is $K_0=\{A,B\}$. A state is viable only if some sequence of available actions can keep the trajectory outside $F$ indefinitely.

Remove candidates without a safe continuation. At $B$, every action has successor $F\notin K_0$, so $B$ must be removed. At $A$, the action “stay” has successor $A\in K_0$, so $A$ remains. The first pruning round gives $K_1=\{A\}$. Repeating the test leaves $A$ because “stay” still returns to $A$; hence $K_2=K_1$.

Following “stay” repeatedly provides an indefinitely safe trajectory from $A$. There is none from $B$, and $F$ is already failed. The viability kernel and its complement in the stated state space are therefore

$$X_V=\{A\},\qquad X_U=\{B,F\}.$$

Check the actions against the kernel, not merely the failure set. At $A$, “stay” sends $A$ back into $X_V$ and preserves viability. “Go” sends $A$ to $B\notin X_V$. Although $B$ is not immediately failed, the next step necessarily sends it to $F$. Thus $A\xrightarrow{\text{go}}B\to F$ is a two-step route to failure, and only “stay” at $A$ preserves the kernel.
